reading.title: The airport and the school yard

A2.text:
Leyla and Aysel were best friends at school in Baku. They did everything together. But when they were eighteen, Aysel's family decided to emigrate to Canada.

The farewell at the airport was very sad. They hugged and cried. “We will keep in touch,” Aysel said. “Every day!” “Say your goodbyes now,” her father said. Leyla waved until Aysel was gone.

At first, they talked every day. Aysel was homesick. She missed Baku, the sea and her friends. But Canada is nine hours behind Baku. Slowly, they talked less. They made new friends. They started to drift apart. After three years, they only sent messages on birthdays.

Ten years later, Leyla got an invitation. There was a school reunion in their old school yard.

On the day, Leyla stood with old classmates. Then she heard a voice. “Leyla?” It was Aysel!

They looked at each other. Then they ran and hugged. They talked for five hours about everything.

“Absence makes the heart grow fonder,” Aysel laughed. “I missed you so much.”

At the end of the evening, they had to part ways again. Aysel was flying back to Canada the next day. It was bittersweet. But this time, they made a plan: a video call every Sunday. And they kept it.

B1.text:
Leyla and Aysel had sat at the same desk from first grade to eleventh. They shared lunches, secrets, exam stress and one terrible haircut. So when Aysel's parents announced, the summer after graduation, that the family would emigrate to Toronto, both girls refused to believe it until the tickets were bought.

The farewell at Heydar Aliyev Airport was the hardest moment of Leyla's eighteen years. At the gate, they held each other until Aysel's father reminded them about the flight. “We'll keep in touch every single day,” Aysel promised. Then she had to say her goodbyes and walk through. Leyla stood at the glass and waved until she could no longer see her.

For the first months, they kept their promise. Aysel was terribly homesick; she missed the sea, her grandmother's cooking and even the Baku wind. They called every night. But Toronto is nine hours behind Baku, and life is busy on both sides of the world. University started. New friends appeared. The calls became weekly, then monthly. Without either of them deciding it, they began to drift apart. By the third year, they were sending each other a heart on birthdays and nothing more.

Ten years later, an invitation arrived: a reunion for their class in the old school yard.

Leyla almost didn't go. When she did, she stood awkwardly with people she hardly recognised — until a voice behind her said, “You still have that terrible haircut.”

She turned around, and there was Aysel.

They talked for five hours on the steps where they used to eat lunch, filling in ten years of gaps.

“They say absence makes the heart grow fonder,” Aysel said. “I never believed it until today.”

At midnight, they had to part ways again; Aysel's flight was at six. The moment was bittersweet, but different from the airport ten years earlier. This time they didn't make big promises. They made a small one: one video call every Sunday.

They haven't missed one since.

B2.text:
Leyla and Aysel had shared a desk from the first grade to the eleventh — lunches, secrets, exam panics and one catastrophic attempt at cutting each other's fringe. So when Aysel's parents announced, the summer after graduation, that the family would emigrate to Toronto, neither girl truly believed it until the tickets had been bought.

The farewell at Heydar Aliyev Airport remained the hardest moment of Leyla's eighteen years. At the security gate, they clung to each other until Aysel's father gently mentioned the boarding time. “We'll keep in touch every single day,” Aysel vowed. Then she had to say her goodbyes and walk through. Leyla stood pressed against the glass, waving long after there was anyone to wave at.

For the first months, the promise held. Aysel was achingly homesick — for the smell of the Caspian, her grandmother's dolma, even the infamous Baku wind — and they spoke every night. But Toronto runs nine hours behind Baku, and life fills whatever space it is given. Lectures began; new friendships formed. Daily calls became weekly, then monthly. Neither of them ever decided it, but they began to drift apart. By the third year, their friendship had dwindled to a heart emoji exchanged on birthdays.

A decade later, an invitation arrived: a class reunion in the old school yard.

Leyla very nearly stayed at home. When she did go, she found herself making stilted conversation with people she barely recognised — until a voice behind her remarked, “Your fringe never recovered, did it?”

She turned, and there was Aysel.

They talked for five hours on the very steps where they had once eaten lunch, laughing, crying and filling in ten years of silence.

“Absence makes the heart grow fonder,” Aysel said eventually. “I always thought that was something people said to feel better. Apparently not.”

At midnight, they had to part ways once more; Aysel's flight left at six. The moment was bittersweet, yet utterly unlike the airport ten years before. This time there were no grand vows. Instead, they made one modest, practical promise: a video call every Sunday, at an hour that suited both cities.

They have not missed one since.
